headline: Schumer says he has the votes. In public, 15 of 55 say so.
summary: Chuck Schumer told reporters Tuesday he has the votes to lead Senate Democrats again. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is running against him, the first contested race for the job in decades. About 15 of the 55 Democrats have backed Schumer in public and four back Van Hollen. The rest are staying quiet. The secret ballot is December 1.

cover_question.q: Why won't they pick a side?

cover_answer: The ballot's secret. Most would rather not be counted yet.
table_question: Your team just won big. Does the captain keep the job automatically?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The senators on one team have to pick a captain, and two of them want the job. One says he already has enough friends on his side to win. The rest will vote on December 1 by writing a name on a folded piece of paper so nobody sees. It's a normal vote. Nobody is in trouble.
5-7.why: A captain and a folded paper. No politics needed.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them a folded piece of paper, a thing they have held, instead of a caucus. Cantor found this age is scared by what looks like a fight, so the slide says twice it is a normal vote. Expect "who wins?" I don't know. Schumer says he does. Ask December 1.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Senate Democrats pick their leader every two years by secret ballot. Chuck Schumer has done the job almost ten years. Chris Van Hollen says it's time for someone new. Schumer says he has the votes, but only about 15 of 55 have said so out loud. A secret ballot is a referee's rule: nobody gets punished for a vote.
8-12.why: Fifteen said yes in public. Thirty-six haven't. That is the gap.
8-12.why_long: A twelve-year-old is working out whether rules get applied fairly, so the script hands them the rule first: every two years, secret ballot, one vote each. Then the chain: 15 said yes in public, four said no, 36 said nothing, and the secret ballot is why they can. Expect "is he lying about the votes?" Nobody can check till Dec. 1.

13-17.script: If you won nine seats for your team, do you keep the captaincy? Senator Hickenlooper thinks so: "We flipped nine seats, and all of a sudden, there's a revolt." Van Hollen says voters want change and he'd push harder to end the Iran war. Second: eight new senators must pick before they're sworn in. Fair?
13-17.why: A win that earns the job, and a demand for change. Both true.
13-17.why_long: A sixteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: Schumer's side won nine seats, and the voters who did it are asking for change. The script hands them Hickenlooper's coin flip and Van Hollen's pitch and lets them argue it, which Kuhn says is how arguing is learned. Expect "why won't Warren say?" The ballot's secret. No need.

5-7.q: Who gets to be the boss?
5-7.a: Whoever gets the most votes from the other senators on December 1. The old captain, Chuck Schumer, says that will be him.

8-12.a: So a senator can vote against the leader and the leader never knows.
Decides which bills get a vote, raises money and recruits candidates.

13-17.q: Why won't they pick a side?
13-17.a: The ballot is secret. Eight must choose before they're sworn in.

13-17.q: Does winning mean you keep the job?
13-17.a: Schumer says 55 seats earns it. Van Hollen says voters want change.
